title: One truth, many names
hookLine: one woman is Mom, Auntie, Doctor and Grandma, depending on who's calling. A Rig Veda verse says the one truth is called by many names
carry: ekam sat: one truth, the wise call it many names
tomorrow: a seer asks Varuna what he did wrong

lines: A VERSE DEEP IN THE RIG VEDA.
cards: At a family party, one woman answers to everything. Her kids call her Mom. Her nephew calls her Auntie.
At the hospital that morning, her patients called her Doctor. Her granddaughter, toddling across the room, calls her something like Nani. Four names, and she turns her head for every one.
Nobody is confused. Each name catches the side of her that person knows. Deep inside the Rig Veda, in a long and puzzling hymn, a verse says something very like this about the divine.

teach.h: MANY GODS, EACH PRAISED IN TURN.
teach.b: The Rig Veda's hymns praise many gods. Agni, the fire. Indra, who wields the thunderbolt and frees the waters.
Varuna, keeper of cosmic order. Mitra, the friend. Soma, the sacred drink.
Ushas, the dawn. A hymn may praise its god in the highest terms, and another hymn may do the same for a different god. Then, in a long riddle-hymn, comes this verse.
In paraphrase: they call it Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni, and the heavenly bird with lovely wings.

teach.h: ONE BEING, CALLED IN MANY WAYS.
teach.b: What is one, the wise speak of in many ways. They call it Agni, Yama, Matarishvan. Ekam sat: one being, one truth, many names.
Readers have heard it more than one way. Some hear all the gods as faces of one divine reality. Vedanta teachers later read it as pointing to Brahman.
Others hear a poet's riddle about the sun, or about speech itself. The verse doesn't settle it. But it has become one of the most quoted lines in Hinduism.
Many Hindus reach for it to explain why one family bows to Krishna, another to Shiva, another to the Goddess, and why they can honor the forms their neighbors love.
And it fits the week: Gaudapada's one self that only seems many, then a fire, a voice, and now many names.

how: Hindus who quote 'ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti', from Rig Veda 1.164.46, use it to say that the one truth is called by many names, and that many forms of the divine are one.

games.q: what does “what the rig veda is” mean?
o: the story of one god who beat all others
hymns to many gods, and a hint of the one
a list of gods ranked from first to last

games.q: the gods and the one — tap the pairs.

s: the Rig Veda's hymns praise only one god
they praise many: Agni, Indra, Varuna, Mitra, Soma, Ushas and more.
one verse says the wise speak of the one in many ways
they call it Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni: what is one, the wise call in many ways.
everyone reads that verse the same way
some hear all gods as faces of one reality, Vedanta reads Brahman, others hear a riddle about the sun or speech.

games.q: you're the poet. you've praised Indra, Varuna and Agni in turn. someone asks: so which one is really it? what do you answer?
o: the wise call the one in many ways.
games.why: the verse names Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni and more, and says: what is one, the wise speak of in many ways.

practice: Silently list the names people call you: your given name, a nickname, a family title like sister or Dad, a work name, and notice how each brings a slightly different you to mind.
Then let the names go quiet one by one and rest in the one who answers to all of them; if you pray, you can call the divine by the name you love best.

wordCard.voice: What the Rig Veda is. Hymns to many gods, and inside them a verse that says the wise call the one truth by many names.

orig.note: Sanskrit: one being, one truth. From Rig Veda 1.164.46: ekam sad vipra bahudha vadanti.

carryVoice: Your line: ekam sat: one truth, the wise call it many names. Many gods praised, and running through them, a hint of the one. See you tomorrow.
